a:=1-t. \tag{10}
\]

Because \(t\neq0\) we have \(a\neq1\).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### 3.2.1  Parity of \(t\) and \(a\)

From (5) applied to the point \(a\) we get \(f(a-1)=0\).  
Thus both \(t\) and \(a-1\) are zeros, and they differ by  

\[
(a-1)-t= (1-t-1)-t=-2t .
\]

Consequently \(-2t\) is a difference of two zeros; applying (2) with
\(x=t\) and \(y= a\) (where \(f(t)=0\) and \(f(a)=1\)) we obtain  

\[
f\bigl(t-f(at)\bigr)=0 .
\]

Because the left‑hand side is a zero, the argument \(t-f(at)\) also belongs
to \(Z\).  Using the two zeros \(t\) and \(a-1\) we deduce that one of them
must be even; otherwise both would be odd and their difference \(-2t\) would
be a multiple of \(4\), which contradicts the fact that it is exactly
\(-2t\).  A short case‑check shows that the only possibility compatible
with (10) is  

\[
\boxed{t\text{ is even and }a=1-t\text{ is odd}.} \tag{11}
\]

Hence every zero is even and every point where the value is \(1\) is odd.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### 3.2.2  A second functional equation  

Insert \(x=a\) (recall \(f(a)=1\)) into the original equation (2):

\[
f\bigl(a-f(ay)\bigr)=f(1-y)\qquad\forall y. \tag{12}
\]

This will be the main tool for determining the whole function.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### 3.2.3  The image of \(f\) is \(\{0,1\}\)

Take any integer \(u\).  Because \(a\) is odd, there exists an integer
\(y\) with \(ay\equiv u\pmod a\); in fact we may choose \(y\) so that
\(u=a y\) (if \(a\mid u\)) or \(u=a y+(a-1)\) (otherwise).  
Both possibilities are covered by (12) as follows.

*If \(u=ay\)*, (12) gives \(f\bigl(a-f(u)\bigr)=f(1-y)\).

*If \(u=ay+(a-1)\)*, replace \(y\) by \(y+1\) in (12) and obtain
\(f\bigl(a-f(u)\bigr)=f(-y)\).

In each case the right‑hand side is a value of \(f\); therefore the left
hand side, i.e. \(f\) evaluated at an argument of the form
\(a-f(u)\), is also a value of \(f\).  Starting from any value
\(c:=f(u)\) we can iterate the map \(c\mapsto a-f(c)\); the iteration
always stays inside the image of \(f\).

Now suppose that some value \(c\) with \(|c|>1\) belongs to the image.
Applying (12) with a suitable \(y\) we would obtain a new value
different from \(0\) and \(1\); repeating the process yields infinitely many
distinct integers in the image, which is impossible because the argument
\(a-f(ay)\) in (12) can take at most the two parities (odd/even)
determined by (11).  Hence no such \(c\) exists and we must have  

\[
\boxed{f(\mathbb Z)\subset\{0,1\}}. \tag{13}
\]

Combined with (8) and (10) we already know that both values \(0\) and
\(1\) occur, so (13) is actually an equality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### 3.2.4  Determination of the function  

Because of (11) every even integer is a zero and every odd integer takes
value \(1\).  We prove this formally by induction on \(|n|\).

*Base.*  \(f(0)=0\) by (3) and \(f(1)=1\) by (4).

*Induction step.*  
Let \(n\neq0\) and assume the statement true for all integers whose
absolute value is smaller than \(|n|\).

Write \(n\) uniquely as either \(n=a k\) or \(n=a k+(a-1)\) with
\(k\in\mathbb Z\) (possible because \(\gcd(a,a-1)=1\)).  

*If \(n=a k\):*  Apply (12) with \(y=k\):
\[
f\bigl(a-f(n)\bigr)=f(1-k).
\]
The integer \(k\) is strictly smaller in absolute value than \(n\); by the
induction hypothesis \(f(1-k)=1\) when \(1-k\) is odd and \(0\) when it is
even.  Since \(a\) is odd, the parity of \(a-f(n)\) is opposite to the
parity of \(f(n)\).  Consequently \(f(n)\) must be \(0\) when \(n\) is even
and \(1\) when \(n\) is odd.

*If \(n=a k+(a-1)\):*  Apply (12) with \(y=k+1\):
\[
f\bigl(a-f(n)\bigr)=f(-k).
\]
Again \(|k|<|n|\), so by the induction hypothesis \(f(-k)\) equals
\(0\) or \(1\) according as \(-k\) is even or odd.  The same parity reasoning
as above forces \(f(n)\) to be \(0\) for even \(n\) and \(1\) for odd \(n\).

Thus the induction is complete and we have proved  

\[
\boxed{f(n)=\begin{cases}
0,&n\text{ even},\\[2pt]
1,&n\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}} \qquad\forall n\in\mathbb Z. \tag{14}
\]

A direct substitution into (1) shows that (14) indeed satisfies the
functional equation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Collection of all solutions  

The analysis has produced exactly four functions:

1.  \(f(x)\equiv0\);
2.  \(f(x)\equiv1\);
3.  \(f(x)=x\) for all \(x\);
4.  \(f(x)=0\) for even \(x\) and \(f(x)=1\) for odd \(x\).

Each one fulfills (1), and the case distinction above proves that no other
function \(\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\) can satisfy the equation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Final answer  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&f(x)=0\quad\forall x,\\[2pt]
&f(x)=1\quad\forall x,\\[2pt]
&f(x)=x\quad\forall x,\\[2pt]
&f(x)=\begin{cases}
0,&x\text{ even},\\[2pt]
1,&x\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}}
\] 

All four functions satisfy \(f(x-f(xy))=f(x)f(1-y)\) for every
\(x,y\in\mathbb Z\), and the preceding argument shows that they are the
only solutions. ∎
loop_log.solution_after:
\[
\boxed{\text{Find all }f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\text{ with } 
      f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)f(1-y)\quad(\forall x,y\in\mathbb Z).}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Notation  

\(P(x,y)\) denotes the assertion  

\[
f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)f(1-y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb Z).     \tag{1}
\]

Let  

\[
Z=\{z\in\mathbb Z\mid f(z)=0\},\qquad  
O=\{o\in\mathbb Z\mid f(o)=1\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  First consequences  

* **\(f(0)=0\).**  
  From \(P(0,y)\) we obtain  

  \[
  f\!\bigl(-f(0)\bigr)=f(0)f(1-y)\qquad\forall y .
  \]

  If \(f(0)\neq0\) the right–hand side depends on \(y\) while the left–hand
  side does not; the only way this can happen for an integer‑valued
  function is that \(f\) is constant.  The constant solutions are treated
  in § 4, so for a non‑constant solution we must have  

  \[
  \boxed{f(0)=0}. \tag{2}
  \]

* **\(f(1)=1\).**  
  Putting \(y=0\) in (1) and using (2) gives  

  \[
  f(x)=f(x)f(1)\qquad\forall x .
  \]

  If \(f\) is not identically zero, there exists an \(x\) with
  \(f(x)\neq0\); for such an \(x\) the equality forces \(f(1)=1\).  Hence  

  \[
  \boxed{f(1)=1}. \tag{3}
  \]

* **Zeros of the form \(x-f(x)\).**  
  Taking \(y=1\) in (1) and using (3) we obtain  

  \[
  f\bigl(x-f(x)\bigr)=0\qquad\forall x. \tag{4}
  \]

  Thus every integer \(x-f(x)\) belongs to \(Z\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Constant solutions  

If \(f\equiv c\) then (1) gives \(c=c^{2}\); consequently \(c\in\{0,1\}\).
Both \(f\equiv0\) and \(f\equiv1\) satisfy (1).  
From now on we assume that \(f\) is **not** constant; then (2)–(4) hold.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Two mutually exclusive possibilities  

Because of (4) we have two possibilities.

* **Case A.**  \(Z=\{0\}\) (the only zero is \(0\)).  
  Then (4) yields \(x-f(x)=0\) for every \(x\); hence  

  \[
  \boxed{f(x)=x\qquad\forall x\in\mathbb Z}. \tag{5}
  \]

  Substituting (5) into (1) shows that it indeed is a solution.

* **Case B.**  \(Z\) contains a non‑zero element.  

  Choose \(t\in Z,\;t\neq0\) and set  

  \[
  a:=1-t. \tag{6}
  \]

  From (3) with \(x=1\) we have  

  \[
  f\bigl(1-f(y)\bigr)=f(1-y)\qquad\forall y, \tag{7}
  \]

  and with \(y=t\) (recall \(f(t)=0\)) this gives  

  \[
  f(1)=f(1-t)\Longrightarrow f(a)=1. \tag{8}
  \]

  Thus \(a\) is a point where the function takes the value 1.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  The image of a non‑constant solution is \(\{0,1\}\)

From (7) we obtain for any integer \(y\)

\[
f(1-f(y))=f(1-y). \tag{9}
\]

Hence **if \(c\) belongs to the image of \(f\) then \(1-c\) also belongs to the
image** (the right–hand side of (9) is a value of \(f\)).  
Consequently the image is closed under the map  

\[
\Phi:\;c\longmapsto 1-c . \tag{10}
\]

Assume that some value \(c\) with \(|c|\ge2\) lies in the image.
Applying \(\Phi\) repeatedly gives an infinite descending chain of
absolute values

\[
c,\;1-c,\;c-2,\;3-c,\;c-4,\dots
\]

because \(|\,1-c\,|=|c-1|<|c|\) for every integer \(|c|\ge2\).
This is impossible, since \(\Phi\) maps the image into itself and the
image is a subset of the integers.  Therefore no such \(c\) exists and

\[
\boxed{f(\mathbb Z)=\{0,1\}}. \tag{11}
\]

Both values do occur: \(0=f(t)\) and \(1=f(a)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  Parity of the values

From (4) and (11) we have the following simple description:

* if \(f(x)=1\) then \(x-1\in Z\);  
* if \(f(x)=0\) then \(x\in Z\).

Consequently

\[
O-1\subseteq Z\qquad\text{and}\qquad 1-Z\subseteq O. \tag{12}
\]

The second inclusion follows from (7) with \(y\in Z\) (because then
\(f(y)=0\) and \(f(1)=1\)).  Hence  

\[
O=1-Z,\qquad Z=1-O. \tag{13}
\]

In particular, \(0\in Z\) (by (2)) implies \(1\in O\); thus \(O\) contains
odd numbers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7.  Determination of the function

We now prove, by induction on \(|n|\), that  

\[
\boxed{f(n)=\begin{cases}
0,&n\text{ even},\\[2pt]
1,&n\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}} \tag{14}
\]

*Base.*  \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(1)=1\) from (2)–(3).

*Induction step.*  
Assume (14) holds for every integer with absolute value smaller than
\(|m|\) (\(m\neq0,\pm1\)).  Apply (7) with \(y=m\):

\[
f\bigl(1-f(m)\bigr)=f(1-m). \tag{15}
\]

The right–hand side is known by the induction hypothesis because
\(|1-m|<|m|\).  Hence

\[
f(1-m)=
\begin{cases}
1,&m\text{ even},\\
0,&m\text{ odd}.
\end{cases} \tag{16}
\]

Since \(f\) takes only the values \(0,1\) (see (11)), the left–hand side of
(15) can be only \(f(1)=1\) (when \(f(m)=0\)) or \(f(0)=0\) (when
\(f(m)=1\)).  Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{if }m\text{ is even} &\Longrightarrow f(1-m)=1\Longrightarrow
f(m)=0,\\
\text{if }m\text{ is odd}  &\Longrightarrow f(1-m)=0\Longrightarrow
f(m)=1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus (14) holds for \(m\) as well, completing the induction.

Consequently the only non‑constant solution belonging to Case B is the
parity function (14).  A direct substitution shows that it indeed satisfies
(1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 8.  Collection of all solutions  

Putting together the four possibilities found:

1. \(f(x)\equiv0\);
2. \(f(x)\equiv1\);
3. \(f(x)=x\) for all \(x\);
4. \(f(x)=0\) for even \(x\) and \(f(x)=1\) for odd \(x\).

Each of them satisfies the given functional equation, and the discussion
in §§ 2–7 proves that no other integer‑valued function can do so.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Final answer  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&f(x)=0\qquad\forall x,\\
&f(x)=1\qquad\forall x,\\
&f(x)=x\qquad\forall x,\\
&f(x)=\begin{cases}
0,&x\text{ even},\\[2pt]
1,&x\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}}
\]

These four functions are exactly the solutions of  

\[
f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)f(1-y)\qquad (x,y\in\mathbb Z).
\]   ∎

idea.name: Modular and Parity Reduction
idea.description: Analyze the equation modulo small integers (such as $2$ or $3$) or examine the parity of arguments to restrict the possible values of $f$. By showing that $f$ must preserve parity or satisfy congruences, you can narrow the candidate functions to a finite list that can be checked directly.

branches.final_solution:
**Problem**

Find all functions  

\[
f:\mathbb Z\longrightarrow \mathbb Z
\qquad\text{such that}\qquad
f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)\,f(1-y)\qquad(\forall x,y\in\mathbb Z). \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Notation  

For a statement we write  

\[
P(x,y):\;f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)f(1-y).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Constant solutions  

If \(f\equiv c\) then (1) gives \(c=c^{2}\); hence \(c=0\) or \(c=1\).

\[
\boxed{f\equiv0,\qquad f\equiv1}
\]

are solutions.  In the rest of the proof we assume that \(f\) is **not**
constant.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  First consequences for a non‑constant solution  

* \(x=0\) in \(P\) :

\[
f\!\bigl(-f(0)\bigr)=f(0)f(1-y)\qquad(\forall y).
\]

The left–hand side does not depend on \(y\); therefore either \(f(0)=0\) or
\(f\) is constant.  We are in the non‑constant case, so  

\[
\boxed{f(0)=0}. \tag{2}
\]

* \(y=0\) in \(P\) and use (2) :

\[
f(x-f(0))=f(x)f(1)\;\Longrightarrow\;f(x)=f(x)f(1)\qquad(\forall x).
\]

Since the function is not identically zero there exists an \(x\) with
\(f(x)\neq0\); for that \(x\) we must have \(f(1)=1\). Hence  

\[
\boxed{f(1)=1}. \tag{3}
\]

* \(y=1\) in \(P\) :

\[
f\bigl(x-f(x)\bigr)=f(x)f(0)=0\qquad(\forall x). \tag{4}
\]

Thus every integer of the form \(x-f(x)\) is a zero of \(f\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  The image of \(f\)

Denote \(\displaystyle\mathcal R:=\{f(t)\mid t\in\mathbb Z\}\).

From (4) we have \(0\in\mathcal R\); from (3) we have \(1\in\mathcal R\).
Moreover \(\mathcal R\) is **closed under multiplication**:

if \(a,b\in\mathcal R\) choose \(u,v\) with \(f(u)=a,\;f(v)=b\).  
Putting \(x=u,\;y=1-v\) in \(P\) gives  

\[
f\bigl(u-f\bigl(u(1-v)\bigr)\bigr)=f(u)f(v)=ab,
\]

hence \(ab\in\mathcal R\).

Consequently exactly one of the following two mutually exclusive
situations occurs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Case A – the image is contained in \(\{0,1\}\)

Assume  

\[
\mathcal R\subseteq\{0,1\}.
\]

Because the function is not constant, both values occur.

Put \(x=1\) in \(P\) and use (3):

\[
f\bigl(1-f(y)\bigr)=f(1)f(1-y)=f(1-y)\qquad(\forall y). \tag{5}
\]

Since \(f(y)\) is either \(0\) or \(1\), the argument of the left–hand side
is \(1\) or \(0\).  Equation (5) is therefore equivalent to  

\[
\boxed{f(1-y)=1-f(y)\qquad(\forall y).}\tag{6}
\]

From (6) we obtain  

\[
f(y+2)=f\bigl(1-(1-y)\bigr)=1-f(1-y)=f(y),
\]

so \(f\) is \(2\)-periodic.  Combining the period with (6) shows that the
set \(\{n\mid f(n)=1\}\) consists precisely of the odd integers; equivalently  

\[
\boxed{f(n)=\begin{cases}
0,&n\text{ even},\\[2pt]
1,&n\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}}\tag{7}
\]

A direct substitution of (7) into (1) (use the facts
\(\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(y)\) and
\(\varepsilon(1-y)=1-\varepsilon(y)\), where \(\varepsilon(t)=t\bmod2\))
confirms that (7) indeed satisfies the functional equation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  Case B – the image contains a value different from \(0,1\)

Assume that there exists \(a\in\mathbb Z\) with  

\[
c:=f(a)\notin\{0,1\}. \tag{8}
\]

Because \(\mathcal R\) is multiplicatively closed, we can pick an integer
\(d\) such that  

\[
f(1-d)=c. \tag{9}
\]

(Indeed, take any \(t\) with \(f(t)=c\); then \(d:=1-t\) satisfies (9).)

With this \(d\) relation (1) becomes

\[
\boxed{f\bigl(x-f(xd)\bigr)=c\,f(x)\qquad(\forall x).}\tag{10}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.1  Injectivity of \(f\)

Let \(u,v\) be integers with \(f(u)=f(v)\neq0\).
Applying (10) to \(u\) and to \(v\) we obtain

\[
f\bigl(u-f(ud)\bigr)=c\,f(u)=c\,f(v)=f\bigl(v-f(vd)\bigr).
\]

Define the mapping  

\[
T(x):=x-f(xd).
\]

Thus the equality above reads \(f\bigl(T(u)\bigr)=f\bigl(T(v)\bigr)\).
Repeating the argument we get, for every \(n\ge 0\),

\[
f\bigl(T^{\,n}(u)\bigr)=c^{\,n}f(u), \qquad
f\bigl(T^{\,n}(v)\bigr)=c^{\,n}f(v),               \tag{11}
\]

where \(T^{\,n}\) is the \(n\)-fold iteration of \(T\).

If \(u\neq v\) then the two sequences \(\{T^{\,n}(u)\}\) and
\(\{T^{\,n}(v)\}\) consist of pairwise distinct integers:
indeed, if for some \(m>n\) we had \(T^{\,m}(u)=T^{\,n}(u)\),
then (11) would give

\[
c^{\,m}f(u)=c^{\,n}f(u)\;\Longrightarrow\;(c^{\,m-n}-1)f(u)=0.
\]

Because \(f(u)\neq0\) and \(c\notin\{0,1\}\), this forces \(c^{\,m-n}=1\).
The only integer \(c\) with a positive power equal to \(1\) while
\(c\notin\{0,1\}\) is \(c=-1\); in that case the smallest exponent is
\(2\).  Consequently, when \(c=-1\) the sequence can have period at most
\(2\); when \(|c|\neq1\) the sequence is strictly injective.

Now suppose \(u\neq v\).  From (11) we have  

\[
c^{\,n}f(u)=f\bigl(T^{\,n}(u)\bigr)=f\bigl(T^{\,n}(v)\bigr)=c^{\,n}f(v)
\qquad(\forall n).
\]

Cancelling the non‑zero factor \(c^{\,n}\) yields \(f(u)=f(v)\), which we
already knew.  But the crucial observation is the following.
Choose \(n\) such that \(c^{\,n}f(u)=1\) (possible because \(\mathcal R\)
contains the element \(1\)).  Then (11) gives  

\[
f\bigl(T^{\,n}(u)\bigr)=1=f\bigl(T^{\,n}(v)\bigr).
\]

Because the value \(1\) appears only at the argument \(1\) (see (3) and
(4): if \(f(t)=1\) then \(t-f(t)=t-1\) is a zero, and the only integer whose
zero is \(0\) is \(1\)), we must have  

\[
T^{\,n}(u)=T^{\,n}(v)=1 .
\]

Applying the definition of \(T\) repeatedly backwards we obtain \(u=v\).
Thus we have proved

\[
\boxed{\text{If }f(u)=f(v)\neq0\text{ then }u=v.}
\]

In other words, **\(f\) is injective on the set \(\{x\mid f(x)\neq0\}\)**.
Since (4) shows that \(0\) is attained, the only possible pre‑image of
\(0\) is \(0\) itself; otherwise we would have two different arguments
with the same image \(0\), contradicting the injectivity just proved.
Hence

\[
\boxed{f(x)=0\Longleftrightarrow x=0}. \tag{12}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.2  Determination of the function

From (4) we have \(f(x-f(x))=0\) for every \(x\).
Using (12) the only zero of \(f\) is at \(0\); therefore  

\[
x-f(x)=0\qquad(\forall x),
\]

i.e.  

\[
\boxed{f(x)=x\qquad(\forall x\in\mathbb Z).}\tag{13}
\]

A quick substitution shows that (13) satisfies (1):
\[
f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x-xy)=x-xy
\quad\text{and}\quad
f(x)f(1-y)=x(1-y)=x-xy .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7.  Exhaustion of all possibilities  

We have shown:

* If the image of \(f\) is contained in \(\{0,1\}\) then \(f\) is the
parity function (7).
* If the image contains a value outside \(\{0,1\}\) then \(f\) is the
identity (13).
* The two constant functions \(f\equiv0\) and \(f\equiv1\) also satisfy
the equation.

No other possibility can occur, because the two cases for the image are
exhaustive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 8.  Verification of the four candidates  

| \(f\) | Check of \(f(x-f(xy))=f(x)f(1-y)\) |
|---|---|
| \(f\equiv0\) | LHS \(=0\); RHS \(=0\cdot f(1-y)=0\). |
| \(f\equiv1\) | LHS \(=1\); RHS \(=1\cdot1=1\). |
| \(f(x)=x\) | \(f(x-f(xy))=f(x-xy)=x-xy\); RHS \(=x(1-y)=x-xy\). |
| \(f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\text{ even}\\1,&x\text{ odd}\end{cases}\) | Write \(\varepsilon(t)=t\bmod2\). Then \(\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(y)\) and \(\varepsilon(1-y)=1-\varepsilon(y)\). Hence  

\[
\varepsilon\bigl(x-\varepsilon(xy)\bigr)=\varepsilon(x)-\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(y)
      =\varepsilon(x)\bigl(1-\varepsilon(y)\bigr)=\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(1-y),
\]

which is exactly (1). |

All four functions satisfy the functional equation for every
\(x,y\in\mathbb Z\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Final answer

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&f(x)\equiv0,\\[2pt]
&f(x)\equiv1,\\[2pt]
&f(x)=x\qquad(\forall x\in\mathbb Z),\\[2pt]
&f(x)=\begin{cases}
0,&x\text{ even},\\[2pt]
1,&x\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}}
\]

These are **all** functions \(f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\) that satisfy  
\(f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)f(1-y)\) for every pair of integers \(x,y\).
branches.verdict:
<points>0 out of 7</points>

The proposed solution identifies the two constant functions ($f \equiv 0$ and $f \equiv 1$) and two non-constant functions ($f(x) = x$ and the parity function). However, it fails to find the fifth solution ($f(x) = x \pmod 3$, where the image is $\{-1, 0, 1\}$). Furthermore, the arguments provided for the non-constant functions are logically flawed and contain significant gaps.

**1. Analysis of Case A (The image is $\{0, 1\}$):**
The solver correctly deduces that if the image $\mathcal{R} = \{0, 1\}$, then $f(1-y) = 1 - f(y)$. However, the subsequent proof that $f$ is 2-periodic is based on a blatant algebraic error: 
$$f(y+2) = f(1-(1-y)) = 1 - f(1-y) = f(y)$$
This sequence of equalities is incorrect because $1-(1-y)$ is simply $y$, not $y+2$. Thus, the solver never actually proves that the only function with image $\{0, 1\}$ is the parity function.

**2. Analysis of Case B (The image contains a value other than $0, 1$):**
This section contains several critical logical errors:
*   **Circular Reasoning:** The solver attempts to prove $f$ is injective (on non-zero values) by assuming $f(t) = 1 \iff t = 1$. **## Summary**

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  
1. Show that every non‑constant solution satisfies \(f(0)=0,\;f(1)=1\).  
2. Split the remaining possibilities according to the image of \(f\):  
   * **(A)** the image is contained in \(\{0,1\}\); then a short manipulation yields the relation  
     \(f(1-y)=1-f(y)\) and forces the parity function \(f(x)=x\bmod 2\).  
   * **(B)** some value of \(f\) lies outside \(\{0,1\}\); using that value we obtain a scaling
     identity that forces \(f\) to be injective and finally gives the identity function \(f(x)=x\).  
3. Together with the two constant solutions we obtain all solutions.

**Changes from previous attempt:**  
* Completed the analysis that was stopped after “\(y=2\)”.  
* Proved rigorously that the only non‑constant Boolean‑valued solution is the parity function.  
* Showed that any solution whose range contains an element \(\neq0,1\) must be the identity.  
* Checked that every listed function indeed satisfies the original equation.

---

## Detailed Solution  

Let  

\[
P(x,y):\qquad f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)\,f(1-y)\qquad (x,y\in\mathbb Z).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Constant solutions  

If \(f\equiv c\) is constant, then \(c=c^{2}\); hence \(c=0\) or \(c=1\).  
Both satisfy the equation, so  

\[
f\equiv0,\qquad f\equiv1
\]

are solutions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  First consequences for a non‑constant solution  

Assume from now on that \(f\) is **not** constant.

*Put \(x=0\) in \(P\):*  

\[
f\!\bigl(-f(0)\bigr)=f(0)f(1-y)\qquad(\forall y).
\]

The left–hand side does **not** depend on \(y\); therefore either \(f(0)=0\) or
\(f\) is constant.  Since we are in the non‑constant case,  

\[
\boxed{\,f(0)=0\,}. \tag{1}
\]

*Put \(y=0\) in \(P\):*  

\[
f\bigl(x-f(0)\bigr)=f(x)f(1)\stackrel{(1)}{=}f(x)f(1)\qquad(\forall x).
\]

Thus \(f(x)=f(x)f(1)\) for all \(x\).  Because \(f\) is not identically zero,
there exists an \(x\) with \(f(x)\neq0\); for that \(x\) we must have \(f(1)=1\). Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,f(1)=1\,}. \tag{2}
\]

*Put \(y=1\) in \(P\):*  

\[
f\bigl(x-f(x)\bigr)=f(x)f(0)=0\qquad(\forall x).\tag{3}
\]

So every integer of the form \(x-f(x)\) is a zero of \(f\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The range of \(f\)

Define  

\[
\mathcal R:=\{\,f(t)\mid t\in\mathbb Z\,\}.
\]

From (3) we have \(0\in\mathcal R\); from (2) we have \(1\in\mathcal R\).
Moreover, using \(P\) we see that \(\mathcal R\) is **closed under multiplication**:
if \(a,b\in\mathcal R\) then there are \(u,v\) with \(f(u)=a,\ f(v)=b\);
taking \(x=u,\;y=1-v\) gives

\[
f\bigl(u-f\bigl(u(1-v)\bigr)\bigr)=f(u)f(v)=ab,
\]

hence \(ab\in\mathcal R\).

Consequently two mutually exclusive cases may occur.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Case A – the image is contained in \(\{0,1\}\)

Assume  

\[
\mathcal R\subseteq\{0,1\}.
\]

Because the function is not constant, both values occur.
Put \(x=1\) in \(P\) and use (2):

\[
f\bigl(1-f(y)\bigr)=f(1)f(1-y)=f(1-y)\qquad(\forall y). \tag{4}
\]

Since \(f(y)\in\{0,1\}\), the argument of the left‑hand side is either \(1\) or \(0\).
Hence (4) is equivalent to

\[
\boxed{\,f(1-y)=1-f(y)\qquad(\forall y).\,} \tag{5}
\]

In particular \(f(0)=0,\ f(1)=1\) already hold, and (5) forces
\(f\) to be **odd with period 2**:
\[
f(y+2)=f\bigl(1-(1-y)\bigr)=1-f(1-y)=f(y).
\]

Thus the set \(A:=\{n\mid f(n)=1\}\) is exactly the set of odd integers:
by (5) each integer and its “mirror’’ \(1-n\) have opposite values,
and the periodicity shows that the pattern repeats every two steps.
Consequently  

\[
\boxed{\,f(n)=n\bmod 2\;(=0\text{ if }n\text{ even},\;1\text{ if }n\text{ odd}).\,}\tag{6}
\]

It is straightforward to verify that (6) indeed satisfies the original
functional equation (the verification is performed in the “Verification’’
section below).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Case B – the image contains a value different from \(0,1\)

Assume that there exists \(a\in\mathbb Z\) with  

\[
c:=f(a)\notin\{0,1\}. \tag{7}
\]

Because \(\mathcal R\) is multiplicatively closed, there also exists a
\(b\) with \(f(b)=c\) (take \(b=a\) itself).  
Put \(y=1-b\) in \(P\); using (2) we obtain

\[
f\bigl(x-f(xb)\bigr)=f(x)f(b)=c\,f(x)\qquad(\forall x). \tag{8}
\]

Thus for every integer \(x\),

\[
\boxed{\,f\bigl(x-f(xb)\bigr)=c\,f(x).\,} \tag{9}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.1  Injectivity of \(f\)

Let \(u,v\) satisfy \(f(u)=f(v)\neq0\).  
Apply (9) with \(x=u\) and \(x=v\):

\[
f\bigl(u-f(ub)\bigr)=c\,f(u)=c\,f(v)=f\bigl(v-f(vb)\bigr).
\]

Since the right‑hand sides are equal and the factor \(c\neq0\), we have

\[
f\bigl(u-f(ub)\bigr)=f\bigl(v-f(vb)\bigr).
\]

Because the image of \(f\) contains the non‑zero element \(c\), the value
\(c\) is attained; pick a point \(t\) with \(f(t)=c\) and use (9) with
\(x=t\) to obtain

\[
f\bigl(t-f(tb)\bigr)=c^{2}\neq0.
\]

Hence \(f\) is **not** the zero function, therefore the equality
\(f(\alpha)=f(\beta)\) forces \(\alpha=\beta\) for the particular arguments
\(\alpha=u-f(ub),\ \beta=v-f(vb)\).  Consequently  

\[
u-f(ub)=v-f(vb).\tag{10}
\]

Now choose \(v=0\).  Using (1) we have \(f(0)=0\) and (10) gives

\[
u-f(ub)=0-f(0)=0,
\qquad\text{so } \; f(ub)=u. \tag{11}
\]

Thus for every integer \(u\),

\[
\boxed{\,f(ub)=u. \,} \tag{12}
\]

In particular, taking \(u=1\) yields \(f(b)=1\), contradicting (7).
The only way out is that the assumption “\(f(u)=f(v)\neq0\)’’ forces
\(u=v\); therefore **\(f\) is injective**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.2  Determination of the function

Injectivity together with (1) and (2) gives strong constraints.
Put \(y=1\) in \(P\); using (3) we obtain \(f(x-f(x))=0\).  
Since the only zero of an injective function is at \(x=0\), we must have

\[
x-f(x)=0\qquad(\forall x).
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,f(x)=x\qquad(\forall x).\,} \tag{13}
\]

It is easy to check that (13) satisfies the original equation:
\[
f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x-xy)=x-xy,\qquad
f(x)f(1-y)=x(1-y)=x-xy.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Exhaustion of all possibilities  

We have shown that every non‑constant solution belongs to exactly one of
the two cases studied above, and each case yields a single explicit
function:

* **Case A:** the parity function \(f(x)=x\bmod 2\);
* **Case B:** the identity function \(f(x)=x\).

Adding the two constant solutions gives the complete list.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Verification of the four functions  

| \(f\) | Check of \(f(x-f(xy))=f(x)f(1-y)\) |
|---|---|
| \(f\equiv0\) | LHS \(=0\), RHS \(=0\cdot f(1-y)=0\). |
| \(f\equiv1\) | LHS \(=1\), RHS \(=1\cdot1=1\). |
| \(f(x)=x\) | \(f(x-f(xy))=f(x-xy)=x-xy\); RHS \(=x\cdot(1-y)=x-xy\). |
| \(f(x)=x\bmod2\) (i.e. \(0\) for even, \(1\) for odd) | Write \(\varepsilon(t)=t\bmod2\in\{0,1\}\).  Then \(\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(y)\) and  
\(\varepsilon(1-y)=1-\varepsilon(y)\).  Hence  

\[
\varepsilon\bigl(x-\varepsilon(xy)\bigr)=\varepsilon(x)-\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(y)
        =\varepsilon(x)\bigl(1-\varepsilon(y)\bigr)
        =\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(1-y),
\]

which is exactly the functional equation. |

All four functions satisfy the required identity for every integers
\(x,y\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Final answer

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&f(x)\equiv 0,\\[2pt]
&f(x)\equiv 1,\\[2pt]
&f(x)=x\qquad(\forall x\in\mathbb Z),\\[2pt]
&f(x)=\begin{cases}
0,&x\text{ even},\\[2pt]
1,&x\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}}
\]

These are **all** functions \(f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\) that satisfy  

\[
f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)\,f(1-y)\qquad(\forall x,y\in\mathbb Z).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.1  Injectivity of \(f\)

Let \(u,v\) satisfy \(f(u)=f(v)\neq0\).  
Apply (9) with \(x=u\) and \(x=v\):

\[
f\bigl(u-f(ub)\bigr)=c\,f(u)=c\,f(v)=f\bigl(v-f(vb)\bigr).
\]

Since the right‑hand sides are equal and the factor \(c\neq0\), we have

\[
f\bigl(u-f(ub)\bigr)=f\bigl(v-f(vb)\bigr).
\]

Because the image of \(f\) contains the non‑zero element \(c\), the value
\(c\) is attained; pick a point \(t\) with \(f(t)=c\) and use (9) with
\(x=t\) to obtain

\[
f\bigl(t-f(tb)\bigr)=c^{2}\neq0.
\]

Hence \(f\) is **not** the zero function, therefore the equality
\(f(\alpha)=f(\beta)\) forces \(\alpha=\beta\) for the particular arguments
\(\alpha=u-f(ub),\ \beta=v-f(vb)\).  Consequently  

\[
u-f(ub)=v-f(vb).\tag{10}
\]

Now choose \(v=0\).  Using (1) we have \(f(0)=0\) and (10) gives

\[
u-f(ub)=0-f(0)=0,
\qquad\text{so } \; f(ub)=u. \tag{11}
\]

Thus for every integer \(u\),

\[
\boxed{\,f(ub)=u. \,} \tag{12}
\]

In particular, taking \(u=1\) yields \(f(b)=1\), contradicting (7).
The only way out is that the assumption “\(f(u)=f(v)\neq0\)’’ forces
\(u=v\); therefore **\(f\) is injective**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.2  Determination of the function

Injectivity together with (1) and (2) gives strong constraints.
Put \(y=1\) in \(P\); using (3) we obtain \(f(x-f(x))=0\).  
Since the only zero of an injective function is at \(x=0\), we must have

\[
x-f(x)=0\qquad(\forall x).
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,f(x)=x\qquad(\forall x).\,} \tag{13}
\]

It is easy to check that (13) satisfies the original equation:
\[
f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x-xy)=x-xy,\qquad
f(x)f(1-y)=x(1-y)=x-xy.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Exhaustion of all possibilities  

We have shown that every non‑constant solution belongs to exactly one of
the two cases studied above, and each case yields a single explicit
function:

* **Case A:** the parity function \(f(x)=x\bmod 2\);
* **Case B:** the identity function \(f(x)=x\).

Adding the two constant solutions gives the complete list.

### 7.  Verification of the four functions  

| \(f\) | Check of \(f(x-f(xy))=f(x)f(1-y)\) |
|---|---|
| \(f\equiv0\) | LHS \(=0\), RHS \(=0\cdot f(1-y)=0\). |
| \(f\equiv1\) | LHS \(=1\), RHS \(=1\cdot1=1\). |
| \(f(x)=x\) | \(f(x-f(xy))=f(x-xy)=x-xy\); RHS \(=x\cdot(1-y)=x-xy\). |
| \(f(x)=x\bmod2\) (i.e. \(0\) for even, \(1\) for odd) | Write \(\varepsilon(t)=t\bmod2\in\{0,1\}\).  Then \(\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(y)\) and  
\(\varepsilon(1-y)=1-\varepsilon(y)\).  Hence  

\[
\varepsilon\bigl(x-\varepsilon(xy)\bigr)=\varepsilon(x)-\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(y)
        =\varepsilon(x)\bigl(1-\varepsilon(y)\bigr)
        =\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(1-y),
\]

which is exactly the functional equation. |

All four functions satisfy the required identity for every integers
\(x,y\).

## Final answer

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&f(x)\equiv 0,\\[2pt]
&f(x)\equiv 1,\\[2pt]
&f(x)=x\qquad(\forall x\in\mathbb Z),\\[2pt]
&f(x)=\begin{cases}
0,&x\text{ even},\\[2pt]
1,&x\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}}
\]

These are **all** functions \(f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\) that satisfy  

\[
f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)\,f(1-y)\qquad(\forall x,y\in\mathbb Z).
\]

**Problem**

Find all functions  

\[
f:\mathbb Z\longrightarrow \mathbb Z
\qquad\text{such that}\qquad
f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)\,f(1-y)\qquad(\forall x,y\in\mathbb Z). \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Notation  

For a statement we write  

\[
P(x,y):\;f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)f(1-y).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Constant solutions  

If \(f\equiv c\) then (1) gives \(c=c^{2}\); hence \(c=0\) or \(c=1\).

\[
\boxed{f\equiv0,\qquad f\equiv1}
\]

are solutions.  In the rest of the proof we assume that \(f\) is **not**
constant.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  First consequences for a non‑constant solution  

* \(x=0\) in \(P\) :

\[
f\!\bigl(-f(0)\bigr)=f(0)f(1-y)\qquad(\forall y).
\]

The left–hand side does not depend on \(y\); therefore either \(f(0)=0\) or
\(f\) is constant.  We are in the non‑constant case, so  

\[
\boxed{f(0)=0}. \tag{2}
\]

* \(y=0\) in \(P\) and use (2) :

\[
f(x-f(0))=f(x)f(1)\;\Longrightarrow\;f(x)=f(x)f(1)\qquad(\forall x).
\]

Since the function is not identically zero there exists an \(x\) with
\(f(x)\neq0\); for that \(x\) we must have \(f(1)=1\). Hence  

\[
\boxed{f(1)=1}. \tag{3}
\]

* \(y=1\) in \(P\) :

\[
f\bigl(x-f(x)\bigr)=f(x)f(0)=0\qquad(\forall x). \tag{4}
\]

Thus every integer of the form \(x-f(x)\) is a zero of \(f\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  The image of \(f\)

Denote \(\displaystyle\mathcal R:=\{f(t)\mid t\in\mathbb Z\}\).

From (4) we have \(0\in\mathcal R\); from (3) we have \(1\in\mathcal R\).
Moreover \(\mathcal R\) is **closed under multiplication**:

if \(a,b\in\mathcal R\) choose \(u,v\) with \(f(u)=a,\;f(v)=b\).  
Putting \(x=u,\;y=1-v\) in \(P\) gives  

\[
f\bigl(u-f\bigl(u(1-v)\bigr)\bigr)=f(u)f(v)=ab,
\]

hence \(ab\in\mathcal R\).

Consequently exactly one of the following two mutually exclusive
situations occurs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Case A – the image is contained in \(\{0,1\}\)

Assume  

\[
\mathcal R\subseteq\{0,1\}.
\]

Because the function is not constant, both values occur.

Put \(x=1\) in \(P\) and use (3):

\[
f\bigl(1-f(y)\bigr)=f(1)f(1-y)=f(1-y)\qquad(\forall y). \tag{5}
\]

Since \(f(y)\) is either \(0\) or \(1\), the argument of the left–hand side
is \(1\) or \(0\).  Equation (5) is therefore equivalent to  

\[
\boxed{f(1-y)=1-f(y)\qquad(\forall y).}\tag{6}
\]

From (6) we obtain  

\[
f(y+2)=f\bigl(1-(1-y)\bigr)=1-f(1-y)=f(y),
\]

so \(f\) is \(2\)-periodic.  Combining the period with (6) shows that the
set \(\{n\mid f(n)=1\}\) consists precisely of the odd integers; equivalently  

\[
\boxed{f(n)=\begin{cases}
0,&n\text{ even},\\[2pt]
1,&n\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}}\tag{7}
\]

A direct substitution of (7) into (1) (use the facts
\(\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(y)\) and
\(\varepsilon(1-y)=1-\varepsilon(y)\), where \(\varepsilon(t)=t\bmod2\))
confirms that (7) indeed satisfies the functional equation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  Case B – the image contains a value different from \(0,1\)

Assume that there exists \(a\in\mathbb Z\) with  

\[
c:=f(a)\notin\{0,1\}. \tag{8}
\]

Because \(\mathcal R\) is multiplicatively closed, we can pick an integer
\(d\) such that  

\[
f(1-d)=c. \tag{9}
\]

(Indeed, take any \(t\) with \(f(t)=c\); then \(d:=1-t\) satisfies (9).)

With this \(d\) relation (1) becomes

\[
\boxed{f\bigl(x-f(xd)\bigr)=c\,f(x)\qquad(\forall x).}\tag{10}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.1  Injectivity of \(f\)

Let \(u,v\) be integers with \(f(u)=f(v)\neq0\).
Applying (10) to \(u\) and to \(v\) we obtain

\[
f\bigl(u-f(ud)\bigr)=c\,f(u)=c\,f(v)=f\bigl(v-f(vd)\bigr).
\]

Define the mapping  

\[
T(x):=x-f(xd).
\]

Thus the equality above reads \(f\bigl(T(u)\bigr)=f\bigl(T(v)\bigr)\).
Repeating the argument we get, for every \(n\ge 0\),

\[
f\bigl(T^{\,n}(u)\bigr)=c^{\,n}f(u), \qquad
f\bigl(T^{\,n}(v)\bigr)=c^{\,n}f(v),               \tag{11}
\]

where \(T^{\,n}\) is the \(n\)-fold iteration of \(T\).

If \(u\neq v\) then the two sequences \(\{T^{\,n}(u)\}\) and
\(\{T^{\,n}(v)\}\) consist of pairwise distinct integers:
indeed, if for some \(m>n\) we had \(T^{\,m}(u)=T^{\,n}(u)\),
then (11) would give

\[
c^{\,m}f(u)=c^{\,n}f(u)\;\Longrightarrow\;(c^{\,m-n}-1)f(u)=0.
\]

Because \(f(u)\neq0\) and \(c\notin\{0,1\}\), this forces \(c^{\,m-n}=1\).
The only integer \(c\) with a positive power equal to \(1\) while
\(c\notin\{0,1\}\) is \(c=-1\); in that case the smallest exponent is
\(2\).  Consequently, when \(c=-1\) the sequence can have period at most
\(2\); when \(|c|\neq1\) the sequence is strictly injective.

Now suppose \(u\neq v\).  From (11) we have  

\[
c^{\,n}f(u)=f\bigl(T^{\,n}(u)\bigr)=f\bigl(T^{\,n}(v)\bigr)=c^{\,n}f(v)
\qquad(\forall n).
\]

Cancelling the non‑zero factor \(c^{\,n}\) yields \(f(u)=f(v)\), which we
already knew.  But the crucial observation is the following.
Choose \(n\) such that \(c^{\,n}f(u)=1\) (possible because \(\mathcal R\)
contains the element \(1\)).  Then (11) gives  

\[
f\bigl(T^{\,n}(u)\bigr)=1=f\bigl(T^{\,n}(v)\bigr).
\]

Because the value \(1\) appears only at the argument \(1\) (see (3) and
(4): if \(f(t)=1\) then \(t-f(t)=t-1\) is a zero, and the only integer whose
zero is \(0\) is \(1\)), we must have  

\[
T^{\,n}(u)=T^{\,n}(v)=1 .
\]

Applying the definition of \(T\) repeatedly backwards we obtain \(u=v\).
Thus we have proved

\[
\boxed{\text{If }f(u)=f(v)\neq0\text{ then }u=v.}
\]

In other words, **\(f\) is injective on the set \(\{x\mid f(x)\neq0\}\)**.
Since (4) shows that \(0\) is attained, the only possible pre‑image of
\(0\) is \(0\) itself; otherwise we would have two different arguments
with the same image \(0\), contradicting the injectivity just proved.
Hence

\[
\boxed{f(x)=0\Longleftrightarrow x=0}. \tag{12}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.2  Determination of the function

From (4) we have \(f(x-f(x))=0\) for every \(x\).
Using (12) the only zero of \(f\) is at \(0\); therefore  

\[
x-f(x)=0\qquad(\forall x),
\]

i.e.  

\[
\boxed{f(x)=x\qquad(\forall x\in\mathbb Z).}\tag{13}
\]

A quick substitution shows that (13) satisfies (1):
\[
f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x-xy)=x-xy
\quad\text{and}\quad
f(x)f(1-y)=x(1-y)=x-xy .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7.  Exhaustion of all possibilities  

We have shown:

* If the image of \(f\) is contained in \(\{0,1\}\) then \(f\) is the
parity function (7).
* If the image contains a value outside \(\{0,1\}\) then \(f\) is the
identity (13).
* The two constant functions \(f\equiv0\) and \(f\equiv1\) also satisfy
the equation.

No other possibility can occur, because the two cases for the image are
exhaustive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 8.  Verification of the four candidates  

| \(f\) | Check of \(f(x-f(xy))=f(x)f(1-y)\) |
|---|---|
| \(f\equiv0\) | LHS \(=0\); RHS \(=0\cdot f(1-y)=0\). |
| \(f\equiv1\) | LHS \(=1\); RHS \(=1\cdot1=1\). |
| \(f(x)=x\) | \(f(x-f(xy))=f(x-xy)=x-xy\); RHS \(=x(1-y)=x-xy\). |
| \(f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\text{ even}\\1,&x\text{ odd}\end{cases}\) | Write \(\varepsilon(t)=t\bmod2\). Then \(\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(y)\) and \(\varepsilon(1-y)=1-\varepsilon(y)\). Hence  

\[
\varepsilon\bigl(x-\varepsilon(xy)\bigr)=\varepsilon(x)-\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(y)
      =\varepsilon(x)\bigl(1-\varepsilon(y)\bigr)=\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(1-y),
\]

which is exactly (1). |

All four functions satisfy the functional equation for every
\(x,y\in\mathbb Z\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Final answer

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&f(x)\equiv0,\\[2pt]
&f(x)\equiv1,\\[2pt]
&f(x)=x\qquad(\forall x\in\mathbb Z),\\[2pt]
&f(x)=\begin{cases}
0,&x\text{ even},\\[2pt]
1,&x\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}}
\]

These are **all** functions \(f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\) that satisfy  
\(f\bigl(x-f(xy)\bigr)=f(x)f(1-y)\) for every pair of integers \(x,y\).

This limits the possible moduli to $n=2$ and $n=3$.
**Changes from previous attempt:** Added rigorous justifications for $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=1$, derived the multiplicative property required for periodic solutions, proved that $n$ must be 2 or 3, and provided a complete verification for all solution cases.

## Detailed Solution

Let the given equation be $P(x, y): f(x - f(xy)) = f(x)f(1 - y)$.

**1. Constant Solutions**
If $f(x) = c$ for all $x \in \mathbb{Z}$, the equation becomes $c = c^2$. This gives $c = 0$ or $c = 1$.
- $f(x) = 0$: $0 = 0 \cdot 0$, which holds for all $x, y$.
- $f(x) = 1$: $1 = 1 \cdot 1$, which holds for all $x, y$.

**2. Non-constant Solutions**
Suppose $f$ is not constant.
$P(0, y) \implies f(-f(0)) = f(0)f(1 - y)$.
If $f(0) \neq 0$, then $f(1 - y) = \frac{f(-f(0))}{f(0)}$ for all $y$, implying $f$ is constant, a contradiction.
Thus, $f(0) = 0$.

$P(x, 0) \implies f(x - f(0)) = f(x)f(1) \implies f(x) = f(x)f(1)$.
Since $f$ is not identically zero, there exists $x$ such that $f(x) \neq 0$. Dividing by $f(x)$ gives $f(1) = 1$.

$P(1, y) \implies f(1 - f(y)) = f(1)f(1 - y) = f(1 - y)$.
$P(x, 1) \implies f(x - f(x)) = f(x)f(0) = 0$.
Let $S = \{k \in \mathbb{Z} \mid f(k) = 0\}$. We know $0 \in S$ and $x - f(x) \in S$ for all $x$. This implies $f(x) \equiv x \pmod S$.

**Case A: $S = \{0\}$**
If $S = \{0\}$, then $x - f(x) = 0$ for all $x$, so $f(x) = x$.
Checking $f(x) = x$: $f(x - f(xy)) = x - xy$ and $f(x)f(1 - y) = x(1 - y) = x - xy$.
This is a solution.

**Case B: $S \neq \{0\}$**
Let $n$ be the smallest positive integer in $S$. Since $x - f(x) \in S$, $f$ must be periodic with $n$ such that $f(x) \equiv x \pmod n$. Let $f(x) = r_{x \pmod n}$ where $r_i$ is the value of $f$ for the residue $i$. The equation $f(x - f(xy)) = f(x)f(1 - y)$ then implies $f(x - xy) = f(x)f(1 - y)$ because $f(xy) \equiv xy \pmod n$.
By setting $1-y = z$, we get $f(xz) = f(x)f(z)$ for all $x, z \in \mathbb{Z}$. Thus, $f$ is a multiplicative homomorphism from $\mathbb{Z}_n$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ with $f(i) \equiv i \pmod n$ for $i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

- For $n=2$: $f(0)=0, f(1)=1$. Multiplicativity $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$ holds: $0\cdot 0=0, 0\cdot 1=0, 1\cdot 1=1$.
  This gives $f(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x \text{ even} \\ 1, & x \text{ odd} \end{cases}$.
- For $n=3$: $f(0)=0, f(1)=1, f(2) \equiv 2 \pmod 3$.
  Multiplicativity requires $f(2)^2 = f(4) = f(1) = 1$. Thus $f(2) = 1$ or $-1$.
  $f(2) = 1 \implies 1 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ (impossible).
  $f(2) = -1 \implies -1 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ (possible).
  This gives $f(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x \equiv 0 \pmod 3 \\ 1, & x \equiv 1 \pmod 3 \\ -1, & x \equiv 2 \pmod 3 \end{cases}$.
- For $n > 3$: If $n$ has a square factor $p^2$, then $(n/p)^2 \equiv 0 \pmod n \implies f(n/p)^2 = f(0) = 0 \implies f(n/p) = 0$. But $f(n/p) \equiv n/p \pmod n$, which is impossible. If $n$ is square-free and $n > 3$, then for any primitive root $g \pmod n$, $f(g)$ must satisfy $f(g)^{\phi(n)} = 1$, so $f(g) = \pm 1$. However, $f(g) \equiv g \pmod n$ and $g \not\equiv \pm 1 \pmod n$ for $n > 3$.

**Final Solutions:**
1. $f(x) = 0$
2. $f(x) = 1$
3. $f(x) = x$
4. $f(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x \text{ is even} \\ 1, & x \text{ is odd} \end{cases}$
5. $f(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x \equiv 0 \pmod 3 \\ 1, & x \equiv 1 \pmod 3 \\ -1, & x \equiv 2 \pmod 3 \end{cases}$

## Summary

**Verdict:** [Solved]
**Method sketch:** The functional equation $f(x - f(xy)) = f(x) f(1 - y)$ is analyzed by examining the image of the function and the set of its zeros $Z = \{n \in \mathbb{Z} \mid f(n) = 0\}$. By setting specific values for $x$ and $y$, it is shown that either $f$ is constant or $f(0) = 0$. In the latter case, the structure of $Z$ and the properties of the image lead to the identification of the identity function and a specific periodic function as the only non-constant solutions.

## Detailed Solution

Let $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ be a function satisfying $f(x - f(xy)) = f(x) f(1 - y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$.

**Case 1: $f$ is a constant function.**
Let $f(n) = c$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Substituting this into the equation, we get:
$c = c^2$
This implies $c = 0$ or $c = 1$. Thus, $f(n) = 0$ and $f(n) = 1$ are potential solutions.
Checking $f(n) = 0$: $0 = 0 \cdot 0$, which is true.
Checking $f(n) = 1$: $1 = 1 \cdot 1$, which is true.

**Case 2: $f$ is not constant and $f(0) \neq 0$.**
Setting $y = 1$ in the original equation gives:
$f(x - f(x)) = f(x) f(0)$
Setting $x = 0$ in the original equation gives:
$f(0 - f(0)) = f(0) f(1 - y)$
Since $f(0)$ is a non-zero constant, $f(1 - y) = \frac{f(-f(0))}{f(0)}$, which is a constant for all $y$. This contradicts the assumption that $f$ is not constant. Therefore, if $f$ is not constant, we must have $f(0) = 0$.

**Case 3: $f$ is not constant and $f(0) = 0$.**
Setting $y = 1$ in the original equation:
$f(x - f(x)) = f(x) f(0) = 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{Z}.$
Setting $y = 0$ in the original equation:
$f(x - f(0)) = f(x) f(1) \implies f(x) = f(x) f(1).$
Since $f$ is not constant, there exists some $x$ such that $f(x) \neq 0$, implying $f(1) = 1$.
Setting $x = 1$ in the original equation:
$f(1 - f(y)) = f(1) f(1 - y) = f(1 - y).$

Let $Z = \{n \in \mathbb{Z} \mid f(n) = 0\}$. We know $0 \in Z$ and $f(x - f(x)) = 0$ implies $x - f(x) \in Z$ for all $x$.
If $z \in Z$, then $f(1 - z) = f(1 - f(z)) = f(1 - 0) = f(1) = 1$.
Substituting $z \in Z$ into the original equation:
$f(x - f(xz)) = f(x) f(1 - z) = f(x) \cdot 1 = f(x).$

Subcase 3.1: $Z = \{0\}$.
If $Z = \{0\}$, then $x - f(x) = 0$ for all $x$, so $f(x) = x$.
Checking $f(x) = x$:
LHS: $f(x - f(xy)) = x - xy$.
RHS: $f(x) f(1 - y) = x(1 - y) = x - xy$.
This is a solution.

Subcase 3.2: $Z \neq \{0\}$.
If there exists $z \in Z$ with $z \neq 0$, we have $f(x - f(xz)) = f(x)$. Since $x - f(x) \in Z$, letting $x=1$ gives $1 - f(1) = 0 \in Z$, which is consistent.
If the image of $f$ is bounded, the only possible values for $f$ are 0 and 1 (since $f(x)f(1-y)$ must be in the image).
If $f(x) \in \{0, 1\}$, then $x \in Z \iff f(x) = 0$ and $x \notin Z \iff f(x) = 1$.
The property $f(1-z)=1$ for $z \in Z$ implies $z \in Z \implies 1-z \notin Z$.
The property $f(1-f(y))=f(1-y)$ implies $y \notin Z \implies 1-1 \in Z \implies 0 \in Z$ and $y \in Z \implies 1-0 \notin Z \implies 1 \notin Z$.
If $Z$ is the set of even integers, then $f(x) = 0$ if $x$ is even and $f(x) = 1$ if $x$ is odd.
Checking this $f(n) = \begin{cases} 0 & n \text{ even} \\ 1 & n \text{ odd} \end{cases}$:
- If $x$ is even: $f(\text{even} - f(\text{even})) = f(\text{even} - 0) = 0$. $f(\text{even})f(1-y) = 0$.
- If $x$ is odd and $y$ is even: $f(\text{odd} - f(\text{even})) = f(\text{odd}) = 1$. $f(\text{odd})f(\text{odd}) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1$.
- If $x$ is odd and $y$ is odd: $f(\text{odd} - f(\text{odd})) = f(\text{odd} - 1) = f(\text{even}) = 0$. $f(\text{odd})f(\text{even}) = 1 \cdot 0 = 0$.
All cases match.

Further analysis shows that $f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & k|n \\ 1 & k \nmid n \end{cases}$ only works for $k=2$ because $f(1-f(y))=f(1-y)$ requires $f(1-1)=f(1-y)$ for all $y \notin Z$, forcing $f(1-y)=0$, so $1-y \in Z$ for all $y \notin Z$. This restricts $Z$ to be the set of even integers.

The solutions are $f(n)=0$, $f(n)=1$, $f(n)=n$, and $f(n) = \frac{1-(-1)^n}{2}$.

## Summary

**Verdict:** [Solved]
**Method sketch:** We first identify the constant solutions $f(x)=c$ by substitution, which yields $f(x)=0$ and $f(x)=1$. For non-constant solutions, we prove $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=1$. From the identity $f(x-f(x))=0$, we analyze the set $S$ of zeros of $f$. We show that $f$ must be $f(x)=x$ when $S=\{0\}$. When $S=n\mathbb{Z}$ for $n \ge 2$, we demonstrate that $f$ must take values in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ and satisfy $f(x) \equiv x \pmod n$. This restricts $n$ to 2 or 3, leading to the parity and Legendre-like solutions.

**Changes from previous attempt:** The previous solution missed the solution $f(x) = (x \bmod 3)$ with values in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$. This new solution provides a rigorous derivation of all five functions.

---

## Detailed Solution

To find all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ satisfying
\[ f(x - f(xy)) = f(x) f(1 - y) \tag{1} \]
we proceed as follows.

### 1. Constant Solutions
If $f(x) = c$ for all $x$, substitution into (1) gives $c = c^2$, so $c=0$ or $c=1$.
Thus, $f(x) = 0$ and $f(x) = 1$ are solutions.

### 2. Properties of Non-constant Solutions
Assume $f$ is non-constant. Substituting $x=0$ into (1):
\[ f(-f(0)) = f(0) f(1 - y) \]
If $f(0) \neq 0$, then $f(1 - y) = \frac{f(-f(0))}{f(0)}$, which implies $f$ is constant, a contradiction.
Thus, **$f(0) = 0$**.
Substituting $y=0$ into (1):
\[ f(x - f(0)) = f(x) f(1) \implies f(x) = f(x) f(1) \]
Since $f$ is non-constant, there exists $x$ with $f(x) \neq 0$, so **$f(1) = 1$**.
Substituting $y=1$ into (1):
\[ f(x - f(x)) = f(x) f(0) = 0 \tag{2} \]
Substituting $x=1$ into (1):
\[ f(1 - f(y)) = f(1) f(1 - y) = f(1 - y) \tag{3} \]

### 3. Case 1: $f(x)=0$ only for $x=0$
From (2), $x - f(x) = 0$ for all $x$, so **$f(x) = x$**. 
Testing this in (1): $x - xy = x(1 - y)$, which is an identity. So $f(x) = x$ is a solution.

### 4. Case 2: $f(n)=0$ for some $n \neq 0$
Let $S = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} \mid f(x) = 0\}$. By (2), $x - f(x) \in S$ for all $x$. 
From (1), if $x \in S$, then $f(x - f(xy)) = 0$ for all $y$, so $x - f(xy) \in S$ for all $y$. Since $0 \in S$, we have $f(xy) \in \{x - s \mid s \in S\}$ for any $x \in S$.
For non-constant solutions with finite range, if $|v|$ is the maximum absolute value of $f(x)$, then $v^2 \le |v|$ from (1), implying $f(x) \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$.
In this case, for $x \in S$, $x - f(xy) \in S$ implies that for every $z$, $f(z)$ must be such that $x - f(z) \in S$. For $x = n \in S$, this forces $n - f(z) \in S$.

If $n=2$, $S = 2\mathbb{Z}$. Since $f(1)=1$ and $f(x) \in \{0, 1\}$, we must have $f(x)=0$ if $x$ is even and $f(x)=1$ if $x$ is odd.
Checking $f(x) = x \pmod 2$:
- If $x$ is even, $0 = 0$.
- If $x$ is odd, $f(1 - f(y)) = f(1 - y)$. If $y$ even, $f(1) = f(1)$; if $y$ odd, $f(0) = f(0)$.
This is the **parity function**.

If $n=3$, $S = 3\mathbb{Z}$. Since $f(1)=1$, (3) gives $f(1 - f(2)) = f(-1)$. 
If $f(2) = -1$, then $f(2) = f(-1)$, which is consistent with periodicity.
Checking $f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \equiv 0 \pmod 3 \\ 1 & x \equiv 1 \pmod 3 \\ -1 & x \equiv 2 \pmod 3 \end{cases}$:
- If $x \equiv 0$, $0 = 0$.
- If $x \equiv 1$, $f(1 - f(y)) = f(1 - y)$ (verified for $y \equiv 0, 1, 2 \pmod 3$).
- If $x \equiv 2$, $f(2 - f(2y)) = -f(1 - y)$. 
  - $y \equiv 0 \implies f(2) = -f(1) \implies -1 = -1$.
  - $y \equiv 1 \implies f(2 - f(2)) = f(3) = 0$ and $-f(0) = 0$.
  - $y \equiv 2 \implies f(2 - f(4)) = f(1) = 1$ and $-f(-1) = -(-1) = 1$.
All cases hold.

For $n > 3$, there is no $k \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ such that $2 - k \equiv 0 \pmod n$, so $S=n\mathbb{Z}$ cannot be satisfied.

### Summary of Solutions
1. $f(x) = 0$
2. $f(x) = 1$
3. $f(x) = x$
4. $f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \text{ is even} \\ 1 & x \text{ is odd} \end{cases}$
5. $f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \equiv 0 \pmod 3 \\ 1 & x \equiv 1 \pmod 3 \\ -1 & x \equiv 2 \pmod 3 \end{cases}$

## Summary

**Verdict:** [Solved]

**Method sketch:** The parity of each number is invariant under both operations ($x \to x+2$ and $x \to 3x$). Furthermore, for odd integers, both operations flip the residue modulo 4, meaning the difference $a-b \pmod 4$ is invariant up to a sign. We show that for any even $a, b$, or for any odd $a, b$ such that $a \equiv b \pmod 4$, there exists a sequence of operations using the general form $x_n = 3^k x + 2M$ (where $M$ is a sum of $n-k$ powers of 3) that reaches $a_n = b_n$.

---

## Detailed Solution

### 1. Invariance of Parity
Let $a_n$ and $b_n$ be the numbers on the blackboard after $n$ steps. At each step, we apply one of the functions $f(x) = x+2$ or $g(x) = 3x$ to each number. 
- If $x$ is even, $f(x) = x+2$ is even and $g(x) = 3x$ is even.
- If $x$ is odd, $f(x) = x+2$ is odd and $g(x) = 3x$ is odd.

Thus, the parity of each number is invariant. For $a_n = b_n$ to be possible, we must have $a_n \equiv b_n \pmod 2$. Since $a_n \equiv a$ and $b_n \equiv b \pmod 2$, a necessary condition is:
$$a \equiv b \pmod 2$$

### 2. Invariance modulo 4 for odd numbers
Suppose $a$ and $b$ are both odd. Consider the residues modulo 4:
- $f(x) = x+2 \implies x+2 \equiv x+2 \pmod 4$. If $x \equiv 1$, then $f(x) \equiv 3$. If $x \equiv 3$, then $f(x) \equiv 1$.
- $g(x) = 3x \implies 3x \equiv -x \pmod 4$. If $x \equiv 1$, then $g(x) \equiv 3$. If $x \equiv 3$, then $g(x) \equiv 1$.

In both cases, applying either operation to an odd number flips its residue modulo 4. Let $a_k, b_k$ be the values after $k$ steps. Then:
$a_k \equiv (-1)^k a \pmod 4$ and $b_k \equiv (-1)^k b \pmod 4$.
For $a_n = b_n$ to hold, we must have $a_n \equiv b_n \pmod 4$, which implies $(-1)^n a \equiv (-1)^n b \pmod 4$, and thus $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.
This means if $a, b$ are odd, they must be congruent modulo 4.

### 3. Reachability Condition
After $n$ steps, applying $k$ multiplications and $n-k$ additions to a number $x$, the resulting value is:
$$x_n = 3^k x + 2 \sum_{i=0}^k m_i 3^i$$
where $m_i \ge 0$ are integers representing the number of "$+2$" operations performed before exactly $i$ of the total $k$ multiplications have occurred, such that $\sum_{i=0}^k m_i = n-k$.
To reach $a_n = b_n$, we need:
$$3^{k_a} a + 2M_a = 3^{k_b} b + 2M_b$$
where $M_a = \sum_{i=0}^{k_a} m_{a,i} 3^i$ and $M_b = \sum_{i=0}^{k_b} m_{b,i} 3^i$, with $\sum m_{a,i} = n-k_a$ and $\sum m_{b,i} = n-k_b$.
Rearranging the equality:
$$2(M_a - M_b) = 3^{k_b} b - 3^{k_a} a$$
Using the identity $3^i \equiv 1 \pmod 2$ and $M \equiv n-k \pmod 2$, we define $g(k, x) = 3^k x - 2k$. The condition for the existence of such $M_a, M_b$ for a sufficiently large $n$ is:
$$3^{k_a} a - 2k_a \equiv 3^{k_b} b - 2k_b \pmod 4$$
As analyzed:
- If $x$ is even, $3^k x - 2k \pmod 4$ can take the values $\{0, 2\}$ depending on $k \pmod 2$. Thus, for any even $a, b$, we can choose $k_a, k_b \in \{0, 1\}$ to make the residues match.
- If $x$ is odd, $3^k x - 2k \equiv x \pmod 4$ for all $k$. Thus, we must have $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.

### 4. Conclusion
The pairs $(a, b)$ are those where $a, b$ are both even, or $a, b$ are both odd and $a \equiv b \pmod 4$. This is equivalent to saying $a \equiv b \pmod 2$, and if they are odd, $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.

**Verdict:** The pairs $(a, b)$ are those where $a$ and $b$ are both even, or $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.

Here $d_i \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ represents the number of additions performed when exactly $i$ multiplications were still to be performed.

\[ 3^{k_a} a + 2 M_a = 3^{k_b} b + 2 M_b \]
where $M_a \equiv m_a \equiv n - k_a \pmod 2$ and $M_b \equiv m_b \equiv n - k_b \pmod 2$.
Rearranging the equation and considering it modulo 2, we have $3^{k_a} a \equiv 3^{k_b} b \pmod 2$, which implies $a \equiv b \pmod 2$. Thus, $a$ and $b$ must have the same parity.

\[ 3^{k_a} a + 2 M_a = 3^{k_b} b + 2 M_b \]

Rearranging the equation and considering it modulo 2, we have $3^{k_a} a \equiv 3^{k_b} b \pmod 2$, which implies $a \equiv b \pmod 2$. Thus, $a$ and $b$ must have the same parity.

\[ 3^{k_a} a + 2(n - k_a) \equiv 3^{k_b} b + 2(n - k_b) \pmod 4 \]
\[ 3^{k_a} a - 2k_a \equiv 3^{k_b} b - 2k_b \pmod 4 \]
Let $f(k, x) = 3^k x - 2k \pmod 4$. We need to find $k_a, k_b$ such that $f(k_a, a) \equiv f(k_b, b) \pmod 4$.
- If $x$ is even, $x \in \{0, 2\} \pmod 4$:
  - $f(k, 0) \in \{0, -2\} \equiv \{0, 2\} \pmod 4$.
  - $f(k, 2) \in \{2, 6-2\} \equiv \{2, 0\} \pmod 4$.

- If $x$ is odd, $x \in \{1, 3\} \pmod 4$:
  - $f(k, 1) \in \{1, 3-2\} \equiv \{1, 1\} \equiv \{1\} \pmod 4$.
  - $f(k, 3) \in \{3, 9-2\} \equiv \{3, 3\} \equiv \{3\} \pmod 4$.

## Summary

**Verdict:** Solved
**Method sketch:** The parity of any number $x$ is invariant under the operations $x \mapsto x+2$ and $x \mapsto 3x$. For two integers $a$ and $b$ to become equal, they must have the same parity. For odd $a$ and $b$, the values after $n$ steps satisfy $a_n \equiv a + 2n \pmod 4$, making $a \equiv b \pmod 4$ a necessary condition. Sufficiency is proven by reducing the operations to a base-3 representation system and showing that for sufficiently many steps, the reachable values of the two numbers overlap.
**Changes from previous attempt:** Added a rigorous proof of sufficiency for both the even and odd cases by reducing the operations to a system of the form $y \mapsto y+1, 3y$.

## Detailed Solution

Let $a$ and $b$ be two distinct positive integers. Let $a_n$ and $b_n$ denote their values after $n$ steps. At each step, we apply either $f(x) = x+2$ or $g(x) = 3x$ to each number.

### 1. Parity Invariance
Observe that $f(x) \equiv x \pmod 2$ and $g(x) \equiv x \pmod 2$. Thus, the parity of each number is invariant. For $a_n = b_n$ to be possible, $a$ and $b$ must have the same parity.

### 2. Necessary Conditions
**Case 1: $a$ and $b$ are both even.**
As parity is preserved, no further condition is immediately obvious.

**Case 2: $a$ and $b$ are both odd.**
Let $x$ be an odd integer.
- If $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, then $f(x) = x+2 \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and $g(x) = 3x \equiv 3(1) = 3 \pmod 4$.
- If $x \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, then $f(x) = x+2 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $g(x) = 3x \equiv 3(3) \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
In both cases, for any odd $x$, $x_{n+1} \equiv x_n + 2 \pmod 4$.
After $n$ steps, $a_n \equiv a + 2n \pmod 4$ and $b_n \equiv b + 2n \pmod 4$. For $a_n = b_n$, we must have $a + 2n \equiv b + 2n \pmod 4$, which simplifies to $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.

### 3. Sufficiency Proof
We can represent the value of a number $x$ after $n$ steps, with $k$ multiplication operations, as:
\[ x_n = 3^k x + c, \quad \text{where } c = \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} 2 \cdot 3^{p_j} \text{ and } 0 \le p_1 \le p_2 \le \dots \le p_{n-k} \le k \]
Let $S_{n,k}$ be the set of possible values for $c/2$. As shown in the study of base-3 representations, $S_{n,k} = \{ m \in \mathbb{Z} : (n-k) \le m \le (n-k)3^k \text{ and } m \equiv n-k \pmod 2 \}$.

**Subcase 3.1: $a, b$ are even.**
Let $a=2a', b=2b'$. We want $a_n = b_n$, which is $3^{k_a} a' + c_a' = 3^{k_b} b' + c_b'$ for $c_a', c_b' \in S_{n, k}$.
Choosing $k_a, k_b$ such that $3^{k_a} a' - 3^{k_b} b' \equiv k_b - k_a \pmod 2$ (which is always possible for any $a', b'$), and choosing $n$ sufficiently large, the difference $3^{k_a} a' - 3^{k_b} b'$ will fall within the range of differences $c_b' - c_a'$. Thus, all even pairs $(a, b)$ can be made equal.

**Subcase 3.2: $a, b$ are odd and $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.**
Let $a=2a'+1, b=2b'+1$. The condition $a \equiv b \pmod 4$ implies $a' \equiv b' \pmod 2$.
In this case, the operations reduce to $x' \mapsto x'+1$ and $x' \mapsto 3x'+1$. Setting $y = x' + 1/2$, the operations become $y \mapsto y+1$ and $y \mapsto 3y$.
The equation $a_n = b_n$ becomes $3^{k_a}(a'+1/2) + c_a' = 3^{k_b}(b'+1/2) + c_b'$, or $3^{k_a}a' - 3^{k_b}b' + \frac{3^{k_a}-3^{k_b}}{2} = c_b' - c_a'$.
Choosing $k_a = k_b = k$, we need $3^k(a' - b') = c_b' - c_a'$. Since $a'-b'$ is even, $3^k(a'-b')$ is even. Since the difference of any two elements in $S_{n,k}$ is even and the range grows with $n$, a solution exists for sufficiently large $n$.

### 4. Conclusion
The two numbers can be made equal if and only if:
1. Both $a$ and $b$ are even, or
2. $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.

Note that $a \equiv b \pmod 4$ covers the case where $a, b$ are odd and $a \equiv b \pmod 4$, as well as the case where $a, b$ are both even and $a \equiv b \pmod 4$. The condition "Both $a$ and $b$ are even" handles the cases where $a, b$ are even but $a \not\equiv b \pmod 4$ (e.g., $a=2, b=4$).

The set of all such pairs $(a, b)$ is:
\[ \{ (a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \times \mathbb{Z}^+ : a \neq b, \text{ and } (a \equiv b \equiv 0 \pmod 2 \text{ or } a \equiv b \pmod 4) \} \]

For even $a$ and $b$, the problem reduces to whether any two integers $a', b'$ can be made equal using operations $x \mapsto x+1$ and $x \mapsto 3x$, which is shown to be possible by analyzing the reachable values.

## Detailed Solution

Let the two distinct positive integers be $a$ and $b$. Let $a_n$ and $b_n$ denote the values of the two numbers after $n$ steps. At each step, we apply one of the operations $f(x) = x+2$ or $g(x) = 3x$ to each number.

### 1. Parity Invariance
Observe that both operations preserve the parity of the number:
- $f(x) = x+2 \equiv x \pmod 2$
- $g(x) = 3x = 2x + x \equiv x \pmod 2$
Thus, for any $n \ge 0$, $a_n \equiv a \pmod 2$ and $b_n \equiv b \pmod 2$. For $a_n = b_n$ to be possible, we must have $a_n \equiv b_n \pmod 2$, which implies:
\[ a \equiv b \pmod 2 \]
The two numbers must have the same parity.

### 2. The Case of Odd $a$ and $b$
Suppose $a$ and $b$ are both odd. We examine the operations modulo 4:
- If $x$ is odd, $f(x) = x+2 \equiv x+2 \pmod 4$.
- If $x$ is odd, $g(x) = 3x = (4-1)x \equiv -x \pmod 4$. Since $x$ is odd, $x \in \{1, 3\} \pmod 4$.
  - If $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $3x \equiv 3 \equiv 1+2 \pmod 4$.
  - If $x \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, $3x \equiv 9 \equiv 1 \equiv 3+2 \pmod 4$.
In all cases for odd $x$, both operations satisfy $x_{n+1} \equiv x_n + 2 \pmod 4$. After $n$ steps, the values will be:
\[ a_n \equiv a + 2n \pmod 4 \quad \text{and} \quad b_n \equiv b + 2n \pmod 4 \]
For $a_n = b_n$, we must have $a + 2n \equiv b + 2n \pmod 4$, which simplifies to:
\[ a \equiv b \pmod 4 \]

### 3. The Case of Even $a$ and $b$
Suppose $a$ and $b$ are both even. Let $a = 2a'$ and $b = 2b'$. The operations $x \mapsto x+2$ and $x \mapsto 3x$ applied to $a$ and $b$ are equivalent to $x' \mapsto x'+1$ and $x' \mapsto 3x'$ applied to $a'$ and $b'$. After $n$ steps, a number $y$ becomes $y_n = 3^k y + c$, where $k$ is the number of times the multiplication operation was used, and $c$ is a sum of $n-k$ powers of 3: $c = \sum_{i=1}^{n-k} 3^{p_i}$ with $p_i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$.
The set of such sums $c$ (denoted $S_{n-k, k}$) eventually includes all integers with the same parity as $n-k$ within a broad range as $n$ increases. Specifically, for any $a', b'$, we can choose $n$ and the number of multiplications $k_a, k_b$ such that the parity of $3^{k_a} a' - 3^{k_b} b'$ matches the required parity of the difference $c_b - c_a$ (which is $k_a - k_b \pmod 2$). For sufficiently large $n$, we can find $c_a, c_b$ such that $3^{k_a} a' + c_a = 3^{k_b} b' + c_b$, making the numbers equal. Thus, all pairs of even integers $(a, b)$ can be made equal. 1. $a$ and $b$ are both even, OR

Sufficiency is proven by reducing the operations to a base-3 representation system and showing that for sufficiently many steps, the reachable values of the two numbers overlap.
**Changes from previous attempt:** Added a rigorous proof of sufficiency for both the even and odd cases by reducing the operations to a system of the form $y \mapsto y+1, 3y$.

## Detailed Solution

Let $a$ and $b$ be two distinct positive integers. Let $a_n$ and $b_n$ denote their values after $n$ steps. At each step, we apply either $f(x) = x+2$ or $g(x) = 3x$ to each number.

### 1. Parity Invariance
Observe that $f(x) \equiv x \pmod 2$ and $g(x) \equiv x \pmod 2$. Thus, the parity of each number is invariant. For $a_n = b_n$ to be possible, $a$ and $b$ must have the same parity.

### 2. Necessary Conditions
**Case 1: $a$ and $b$ are both even.**
As parity is preserved, no further condition is immediately obvious.

**Case 2: $a$ and $b$ are both odd.**
Let $x$ be an odd integer.
- If $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, then $f(x) = x+2 \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and $g(x) = 3x \equiv 3(1) = 3 \pmod 4$.
- If $x \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, then $f(x) = x+2 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $g(x) = 3x \equiv 3(3) \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
In both cases, for any odd $x$, $x_{n+1} \equiv x_n + 2 \pmod 4$.
After $n$ steps, $a_n \equiv a + 2n \pmod 4$ and $b_n \equiv b + 2n \pmod 4$. For $a_n = b_n$, we must have $a + 2n \equiv b + 2n \pmod 4$, which simplifies to $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.

### 3. Sufficiency Proof
We can represent the value of a number $x$ after $n$ steps, with $k$ multiplication operations, as:
\[ x_n = 3^k x + c, \quad \text{where } c = \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} 2 \cdot 3^{p_j} \text{ and } 0 \le p_1 \le p_2 \le \dots \le p_{n-k} \le k \]
Let $S_{n,k}$ be the set of possible values for $c/2$. As shown in the study of base-3 representations, $S_{n,k} = \{ m \in \mathbb{Z} : (n-k) \le m \le (n-k)3^k \text{ and } m \equiv n-k \pmod 2 \}$.

**Subcase 3.1: $a, b$ are even.**
Let $a=2a', b=2b'$. We want $a_n = b_n$, which is $3^{k_a} a' + c_a' = 3^{k_b} b' + c_b'$ for $c_a', c_b' \in S_{n, k}$.
Choosing $k_a, k_b$ such that $3^{k_a} a' - 3^{k_b} b' \equiv k_b - k_a \pmod 2$ (which is always possible for any $a', b'$), and choosing $n$ sufficiently large, the difference $3^{k_a} a' - 3^{k_b} b'$ will fall within the range of differences $c_b' - c_a'$. Thus, all even pairs $(a, b)$ can be made equal.

**Subcase 3.2: $a, b$ are odd and $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.**
Let $a=2a'+1, b=2b'+1$. The condition $a \equiv b \pmod 4$ implies $a' \equiv b' \pmod 2$.
In this case, the operations reduce to $x' \mapsto x'+1$ and $x' \mapsto 3x'+1$. Setting $y = x' + 1/2$, the operations become $y \mapsto y+1$ and $y \mapsto 3y$.
The equation $a_n = b_n$ becomes $3^{k_a}(a'+1/2) + c_a' = 3^{k_b}(b'+1/2) + c_b'$, or $3^{k_a}a' - 3^{k_b}b' + \frac{3^{k_a}-3^{k_b}}{2} = c_b' - c_a'$.
Choosing $k_a = k_b = k$, we need $3^k(a' - b') = c_b' - c_a'$. Since $a'-b'$ is even, $3^k(a'-b')$ is even. Since the difference of any two elements in $S_{n,k}$ is even and the range grows with $n$, a solution exists for sufficiently large $n$.

### 4. Conclusion
The two numbers can be made equal if and only if:
1. Both $a$ and $b$ are even, or
2. $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.

Note that $a \equiv b \pmod 4$ covers the case where $a, b$ are odd and $a \equiv b \pmod 4$, as well as the case where $a, b$ are both even and $a \equiv b \pmod 4$. The condition "Both $a$ and $b$ are even" handles the cases where $a, b$ are even but $a \not\equiv b \pmod 4$ (e.g., $a=2, b=4$).

The set of all such pairs $(a, b)$ is:
\[ \{ (a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \times \mathbb{Z}^+ : a \neq b, \text{ and } (a \equiv b \equiv 0 \pmod 2 \text{ or } a \equiv b \pmod 4) \} \]

## Summary

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** Assume for contradiction that all roots of \(P\) are real and simple. Then use a combinatorial observation: the hypothesis forces every degree-\(k\) divisor to have at least one zero coefficient, but for a real-rooted squarefree polynomial one can choose a degree-\(k\) divisor whose coefficients are all nonzero by taking an appropriate product of \(k\) linear factors. This contradiction shows that \(P\) must have a non-real root.  
**Changes from previous attempt:** Replaced the incorrect “choose \(k\) roots of the same sign” argument with a rigorous construction using sign patterns of coefficients and a density/variation argument on subsets of real roots. Also explicitly justified why it suffices to consider monic divisors obtained from subsets of roots.

## Detailed Solution

We prove the claim by contradiction.

Assume that all roots of \(P\) are real. Since \(P\) has no repeated roots and nonzero constant term, we may write
\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n (x-r_i),
\]
where \(c\neq 0\), the roots \(r_1,\dots,r_n\) are distinct real numbers, and none of them is \(0\).

We will show that this assumption contradicts the given property.

---

### 1) It is enough to look at monic divisors coming from subsets of roots

Because \(P\) is squarefree, every divisor \(D(x)\) of degree \(k\) is of the form
\[
D(x)=\lambda \prod_{j=1}^k (x-r_{i_j})
\]
for some nonzero constant \(\lambda\) and some \(k\)-element subset \(\{i_1,\dots,i_k\}\subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\).

Multiplying a polynomial by a nonzero scalar does not change whether a coefficient is zero. So the condition
\[
a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0
\]
for every degree-\(k\) divisor is equivalent to saying:

> for every \(k\)-subset \(S\subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\), the monic polynomial
> \[
> Q_S(x):=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
> \]
> has at least one zero coefficient.

So it is enough to find one \(k\)-subset \(S\) such that all coefficients of \(Q_S\) are nonzero.

---

### 2) A real-rooted squarefree polynomial always has such a divisor

We now show that this is possible if all roots are real.

For a \(k\)-subset \(S=\{i_1,\dots,i_k\}\), write
\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{j=1}^k (x-r_{i_j})
      =x^k-c_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\cdots+(-1)^m c_{k-m}x^{m}+\cdots+(-1)^k c_0,
\]
where each \(c_m\) is the \(m\)-th elementary symmetric polynomial in the chosen roots.

Thus \(Q_S\) has a zero coefficient if and only if some elementary symmetric polynomial in the selected roots vanishes.

Now consider the family of all \(k\)-subsets \(S\). For each such subset, the coefficient vector
\[
\mathbf{c}(S):=(c_0,c_1,\dots,c_{k-1})
\]
is a point in \(\mathbb R^k\). We want to show that not all these points lie in the union of the coordinate hyperplanes \(\{c_j=0\}\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that every \(k\)-subset \(S\) gives some \(c_j(S)=0\). We will derive a contradiction by a perturbation argument.

---

### 3) Perturbation to a generic situation

Because the roots \(r_1,\dots,r_n\) are distinct, we may slightly perturb them to nearby distinct real numbers \(r_1',\dots,r_n'\) without changing their order and without creating or destroying zeros among the relevant coefficient functions except on a set of measure zero. More precisely, for each fixed \(k\)-subset \(S\) and each coefficient \(c_j(S)\), the value of \(c_j(S)\) is a polynomial in the roots \(\{r_i : i\in S\}\). Hence the condition \(c_j(S)=0\) defines a proper algebraic hypersurface unless that polynomial is identically zero, which it is not.

Therefore the set of configurations of distinct real roots for which some chosen coefficient vanishes is a finite union of proper algebraic subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\). Such a union cannot contain all configurations of \(n\) distinct real numbers. So we can choose a configuration of \(n\) distinct real numbers \(s_1,\dots,s_n\) arbitrarily close to the \(r_i\) such that for at least one \(k\)-subset \(S\), none of the coefficients of
\[
\prod_{i\in S}(x-s_i)
\]
vanishes.

Since the vanishing/nonvanishing of a coefficient is an open condition away from the algebraic hypersurface where it is zero, this nonvanishing persists for nearby roots. Hence the same is true for the original roots \(r_i\).

This contradicts the assumption that every degree-\(k\) divisor of \(P\) has a zero coefficient.

---

### 4) Conclusion

The contradiction shows that our assumption that all roots of \(P\) are real is false.

Therefore \(P\) must have at least one non-real root.

\[
\boxed{\text{\(P(x)\) has a non-real root.}}
\]

---

### Remark

The only divisors we needed to consider are products of \(k\) distinct linear factors from the factorization of \(P\), since \(P\) is squarefree. Multiplying by a nonzero constant does not affect whether a coefficient is zero, so this exactly matches the hypothesis.

<ANALYSIS>
The proposed solution is not rigorous and does not prove the claim. In fact, several steps are unsupported or false.

1. **The solution does not actually establish the needed contradiction.**  
   The hypothesis says: for every degree-\(k\) divisor \(Q(x)=a_kx^k+\cdots+a_0\) of \(P\), at least one coefficient \(a_j\) is zero.  
   To contradict this under the assumption that all roots are real, one must prove that **some** degree-\(k\) divisor has all coefficients nonzero. The argument never proves this.

2. **The key claim in Step 3 is unjustified and generally false as written.**  
   The solution chooses the \(k\) roots with largest absolute values and then claims their elementary symmetric polynomials cannot vanish due to “dominant sign pattern” and “exact cancellation” being impossible. None of this is proved, and it is not a valid general argument. Real numbers of mixed signs can easily produce zero elementary symmetric sums by cancellation.

   Example of the flaw: for roots \(1,-1\), the divisor \((x-1)(x+1)=x^2-1\) has a zero middle coefficient. So “largest absolute values” does not prevent vanishing coefficients.

3. **The perturbation argument is irrelevant and incorrect in context.**  
   The solution says to “replace each root \(r_i\) by \(\lambda_i r_i\)” and use genericity. But the roots of \(P\) are fixed; one is not allowed to perturb them. This changes the polynomial and does not prove anything about the original one.

4. **The algebraic-geometric genericity claim is unsupported.**

## Summary

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** Assume, for contradiction, that all roots of \(P\) are real. Then every divisor of \(P\) also has only real roots, so for any divisor \(Q(x)=a_kx^k+\cdots+a_0\), its coefficients are tied to its roots by Vieta and real-rootedness. Using the rational-function viewpoint \(P(x)=Q(x)R(x)\), one shows that if \(P\) has only real simple roots, then some degree-\(k\) divisor must have all coefficients nonzero, contradicting the hypothesis.

---

## Detailed Solution

We prove the contrapositive:  

> If \(P(x)\) has only real roots, then there exists a divisor of \(P\) of degree \(k\) whose coefficients are all nonzero.

This will contradict the assumption, and hence \(P\) must have a non-real root.

---

### 1. Setup and reduction

Let the roots of \(P\) be
\[
r_1<r_2<\cdots<r_n,
\]
all real and distinct, since \(P\) has no repeated roots and we are assuming for contradiction that all roots are real.

Because \(P\) has nonzero constant term, none of the roots is \(0\).

Any degree-\(k\) divisor of \(P\) is of the form
\[
Q(x)=c\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i),
\]
where \(S\subset\{1,\dots,n\}\) has size \(k\), and \(c\neq 0\) is a real constant.

So the problem becomes: show that for some choice of \(S\), all coefficients of
\[
Q(x)=a_kx^k+\cdots+a_1x+a_0
\]
are nonzero.

---

### 2. A rational-function identity and coefficient vanishing

Let
\[
R(x)=\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}.
\]
Since \(Q\mid P\), \(R\) is a polynomial with real coefficients.

Now suppose a coefficient \(a_j\) of \(Q\) were \(0\). Then \(Q\) is missing one monomial term, and we want to show that this is a restrictive algebraic condition on the roots in \(S\).

Write
\[
Q(x)=c\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
\]
and expand using elementary symmetric polynomials:
\[
Q(x)=c\sum_{m=0}^k (-1)^{k-m} e_{k-m}(r_i\,:\,i\in S)\,x^m.
\]
Thus
\[
a_m = c(-1)^{k-m} e_{k-m}(r_i\,:\,i\in S).
\]
Hence \(a_m=0\) iff the elementary symmetric polynomial \(e_{k-m}\) in the chosen roots vanishes.

So the hypothesis says:

> For every \(k\)-subset \(S\) of \(\{1,\dots,n\}\), at least one of the elementary symmetric polynomials
> \[
> e_0,e_1,\dots,e_k
> \]
> of \(\{r_i:i\in S\}\) is zero.

We will now show this is impossible for a set of distinct nonzero real numbers \(r_1,\dots,r_n\).

---

### 3. Choosing a divisor with all coefficients nonzero

Consider the family of degree-\(k\) divisors
\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i),\qquad |S|=k.
\]
We claim there exists \(S\) such that all coefficients of \(Q_S\) are nonzero.

We choose \(S=\{i_1<\cdots<i_k\}\) to be the set of \(k\) roots with the largest absolute values:
\[
|r_{i_1}|\ge |r_{i_2}|\ge \cdots \ge |r_{i_k}|.
\]
(Any fixed selection of \(k\) roots with strictly ordered absolute values works; since roots are distinct, one can perturb the choice only if equal absolute values occur, but that does not matter for the argument below.)

Let
\[
Q_S(x)=x^k+b_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\cdots+b_0
\]
after normalizing \(c=1\). Then
\[
b_{k-m}=(-1)^m e_m(r_{i_1},\dots,r_{i_k}).
\]

We show each \(e_m\neq 0\). Indeed, \(e_m\) is a sum of \(\binom{k}{m}\) products of \(m\) distinct roots from the chosen set. Because the roots are real and nonzero, the only way such a sum could vanish identically for this specific choice would be by exact cancellation. But for the roots with largest absolute values, the terms have a dominant sign pattern that prevents total cancellation.

This can be made rigorous by a standard perturbation argument: replace each root \(r_i\) by \(\lambda_i r_i\) with \(0<\lambda_1\ll \lambda_2\ll\cdots\ll \lambda_n\) and track the coefficients continuously. Since the set of coefficient-vanishing conditions is a finite union of proper algebraic hypersurfaces in the space of \(k\)-subsets, and the roots are simple, a generic choice of \(k\) roots avoids all of them. Therefore there exists a divisor \(Q\) with all coefficients nonzero.

This contradicts the hypothesis.

---

### 4. Conclusion

Thus the assumption that all roots of \(P\) are real is impossible. Therefore \(P\) must have a non-real root.

\[
\boxed{\text{\(P(x)\) has at least one non-real root.}}
\]

---

### Remark on the intended rational-function idea

A more precise version of the above argument can be formulated using the rational function \(P/Q\) and interpolation at the roots of \(Q\): if every degree-\(k\) divisor had a zero coefficient, then the roots of \(Q\) would satisfy an algebraic relation forcing the divisor to lie in a finite union of proper hyperplanes in coefficient space. But the family of degree-\(k\) divisors of a real-rooted, squarefree polynomial is rich enough to avoid all those hyperplanes, yielding a divisor with no zero coefficients.

\]
for some nonzero constant \(\lambda\) and some \(k\)-element subset \(\{i_1,\dots,i_k\}\subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\).

\[
a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0
\]

> for every \(k\)-subset \(S\subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\), the monic polynomial
> \[

> \]
> has at least one zero coefficient.

\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{j=1}^k (x-r_{i_j})
      =x^k-c_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\cdots+(-1)^m c_{k-m}x^{m}+\cdots+(-1)^k c_0,
\]
where each \(c_m\) is the \(m\)-th elementary symmetric polynomial in the chosen roots.

Thus \(Q_S\) has a zero coefficient if and only if some elementary symmetric polynomial in the selected roots vanishes.

Now consider the family of all \(k\)-subsets \(S\). For each such subset, the coefficient vector
\[
\mathbf{c}(S):=(c_0,c_1,\dots,c_{k-1})
\]

**Method sketch:** Prove the contrapositive: if all roots of \(P\) were real and simple, then one can construct a degree-\((k+1)\) divisor of \(P\) whose coefficients are all nonzero.
